title: Prices and choices
summary: Three economic ideas behind every IAM: prices balance markets, a carbon price changes who wins, and discounting weighs the future.
outcomes: You can explain how a market price balances supply and demand.
You can add a carbon price to a technology's cost and say which option wins.
You can explain why real models share a market instead of picking one winner.
You can discount a future amount and say why the rate matters.
narration_en: Only three ideas from economics are needed to read an integrated assessment model. First, a market price keeps moving until what is offered equals what is wanted, like a farmers market at closing time. That balancing price is called the equilibrium. GCAM finds such a price for every fuel and crop, in every region, in each time step. Second, a carbon price adds a charge to every option in proportion to its emissions. Coal costs sixty dollars a megawatt hour and emits zero point nine tonnes of carbon dioxide; with a fifty dollar carbon price it costs one hundred and five. Gas rises to ninety. Solar stays at eighty, because it emits nothing. The winner changes. Real models rarely give everything to the cheapest option. They share the market, so cheaper options get bigger shares. Third, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later. Discounting turns future amounts into today's money. At three percent a year, one hundred dollars of damage in a hundred years is worth only about five dollars today; at one and a half percent, about twenty two dollars. The rate a modeller chooses changes how much the future counts.
narration_ar: لا يلزم من علم الاقتصاد إلا ثلاث أفكار لقراءة نموذج التقييم المتكامل. الأولى أن سعر السوق يظل يتحرك حتى يتساوى المعروض مع المطلوب، كسوق الخضار عند الإغلاق. ويسمى هذا السعر المتوازن «سعر التوازن». ويجد نموذج GCAM سعرًا كهذا لكل وقود ومحصول، في كل منطقة، وفي كل خطوة زمنية. والثانية أن سعر الكربون يضيف رسمًا إلى كل خيار بقدر انبعاثاته. فالفحم يكلف ستين دولارًا للميغاواط ساعة ويطلق تسعة أعشار الطن من ثاني أكسيد الكربون، فإذا فُرض سعر كربون قدره خمسون دولارًا صارت تكلفته مئة وخمسة دولارات، وارتفع الغاز إلى تسعين، وبقيت الطاقة الشمسية عند ثمانين لأنها لا تطلق شيئًا، فيتغير الفائز. ونادرًا ما تمنح النماذج الحقيقية السوق كله للخيار الأرخص، بل تقسّمه، فينال الأرخص حصة أكبر. والثالثة أن الدولار اليوم أثمن من الدولار غدًا، و«الخصم» يحوّل المبالغ المستقبلية إلى قيمتها اليوم. فبمعدل ثلاثة في المئة سنويًا لا تساوي أضرار قيمتها مئة دولار بعد مئة عام إلا نحو خمسة دولارات اليوم، وبمعدل واحد ونصف في المئة نحو اثنين وعشرين دولارًا. فالمعدل الذي يختاره صاحب النموذج يغيّر وزن المستقبل في الحساب.

diagram.title: How prices drive choices in an IAM
diagram.caption: Notice the loop: costs set prices, prices set shares, shares set emissions, and a carbon price feeds emissions back into costs.

nodes.label: Demand
nodes.detail: Buyers want less when the price is high. Toy lab numbers: demand = 1000 − 4 × price.

nodes.label: Supply
nodes.detail: Sellers offer more when the price is high. Toy numbers: supply = 6 × price.

nodes.label: Technology costs
nodes.detail: Illustrative costs in $ per MWh before any carbon price.

nodes.label: Carbon price
nodes.detail: New cost = start cost + emission factor × carbon price. At $50: coal 105, gas 90, solar 80.

nodes.label: Market shares
nodes.detail: GCAM does not give everything to the cheapest option. It shares the market by relative cost (a logit choice, Go 2).

nodes.label: Discounting
nodes.detail: Value today = future amount ÷ (1 + rate)^years. $100 in 100 years: $22.56 at 1.5%, $5.20 at 3%, $0.76 at 5%.

tour.text: Idea one: buyers want less when prices are high; sellers offer more.
The price moves until they match: the equilibrium. In the toy market, price 100 and quantity 600.
Idea two: a carbon price adds emissions × price to each option's cost. Coal is hit hardest, solar not at all.
Cheaper options win bigger shares. Real models share the market rather than pick a single winner.
Idea three: discounting. The rate decides how much future damage counts today, and so how strong a policy looks worthwhile.

sections.heading: Prices balance markets
sections.html:
Think of a farmers' market at closing time. If tomatoes pile up unsold, sellers cut the price; if they sell out by noon, they raise it next week. The price keeps moving until what is offered equals what is wanted: the equilibrium.

Toy numbers from the course lab: demand = 1000 − 4p and supply = 6p. Setting them equal, 1000 = 10p, so p = 100 and quantity = 600. GCAM finds a balancing price like this for every fuel and crop, in every region, in every time step.

sections.heading: A carbon price changes who wins
sections.html:
new cost = start cost + emission factor × carbon price
TechnologyCost, $/MWht CO2/MWhWith $50/t
Coal600.960 + 0.9 × 50 = 105
Gas700.470 + 0.4 × 50 = 90
Solar80080

Gas beats coal above $20 per tonne; solar beats gas above $25 per tonne (illustrative costs).

sections.heading: Real models share the market
sections.html: In the toy table the cheapest option takes everything. Real people and firms do not all choose the same thing: costs differ by place, and tastes differ. So GCAM shares each market among options by their relative cost: the cheapest gets the biggest share, but not all of it. You will meet the rule, called a logit, in Go 2.

sections.heading: Discounting weighs the future
sections.html:
A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later: you could invest it or use it now. Discounting turns future money into today's value:

value today = future amount ÷ (1 + r)years

$100 of climate damage in 100 years is worth $22.56 today at 1.5%, $5.20 at 3% and $0.76 at 5%. One number chosen by the modeller changes the value of the future roughly thirtyfold. Cost-benefit models such as DICE use discounting to weigh cutting now against damage later; process models use prices to decide which technologies supply each market.

callouts.title: Common trap
callouts.html: "A carbon price makes everything more expensive." Only options that emit. Solar's cost does not change. And "a high discount rate means we care more about the future" is backwards: a high rate makes the future count less.

callouts.title: Try it now
callouts.html: At a carbon price of $22 per tonne, which technology is cheapest? (Answer: coal 79.8, gas 78.8, solar 80, so gas.)

callouts.title: A useful mental model
callouts.html: A carbon price is a toll charged in proportion to the smoke each option makes. Everything else in the model reacts to the new tolls.

explorer.intro: Move the carbon price and watch which technology becomes cheapest, and how the market price and quantity shift.
explorer.predict: At what carbon price does solar first become the cheapest option? Write your guess, then slide to check.

code.title: Which plant wins at each carbon price?
code.source:
# Which power plant wins? Cost with a carbon price = base cost + emissions x price
plants = {"coal": (60, 0.9), "gas": (70, 0.4), "solar": (80, 0.0)}  # $/MWh, t CO2/MWh

for price in (0, 22, 50):
    costs = {k: base + ef * price for k, (base, ef) in plants.items()}
    winner = min(costs, key=costs.get)
    shown = ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.1f}" for k, v in costs.items())
    print(f"carbon price ${price:>2}/t: {shown} -> cheapest: {winner}")
code.explain: Press Run. Then add a price of 30, or give coal carbon capture by lowering its 0.9 to 0.1, and predict the winner first. Costs are illustrative.
code.expected:
carbon price $ 0/t: coal 60.0, gas 70.0, solar 80.0 -> cheapest: coal
carbon price $22/t: coal 79.8, gas 78.8, solar 80.0 -> cheapest: gas
carbon price $50/t: coal 105.0, gas 90.0, solar 80.0 -> cheapest: solar

code.title: What is future damage worth today?
code.source:
# What is $100 of damage in 100 years worth today?
for rate in (0.015, 0.03, 0.05):
    today = 100 / (1 + rate) ** 100
    print(f"discount rate {rate:.1%}: ${today:.2f}")
code.explain: Press Run. Change 100 years to 30 and compare: discounting matters most for the far future.
code.expected:
discount rate 1.5%: $22.56
discount rate 3.0%: $5.20
discount rate 5.0%: $0.76

takeaways: Prices move until supply equals demand: the equilibrium.
A carbon price adds emission factor × price to each option's cost, so clean options gain.
Toy break-evens: gas beats coal above $20/t, solar beats gas above $25/t.
Real IAMs share markets by relative cost instead of picking one winner.
Discounting divides future values by (1 + r)^years; the chosen rate changes how much the future counts.

quiz.explain: The charge is emission factor × price, and 0 × anything is 0.

options: The cheapest one takes the whole market
It shares the market, giving cheaper options bigger shares
The modeller fixes every share by hand
quiz.explain: GCAM shares markets by relative cost with a logit rule; cheaper options get bigger, but not complete, shares.

glossary.def: The price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer.
A charge per tonne of CO2 emitted, which raises the cost of each option in proportion to its emissions.
Tonnes of CO2 released per unit of output, for example 0.9 t CO2 per MWh from a coal plant.
The yearly rate used to convert future money into today's value; a higher rate makes the future count less.
What a future amount is worth today: future amount ÷ (1 + r)^years.
The fraction of a market supplied by one option, for example solar's share of new electricity.
